props.text: Architectural typologies
Four ways we work with site, light, and existing structure.

Inward gardens that anchor daily domestic rhythm.
Rather than pushing outdoor space to a residual lawn, our residential commissions wrap rooms around a sheltered court that moderates wind, rain and seasonal sun.
Three-sided solar orientation
Daylight enters living and kitchen spaces from both the street edge and the planted central court.
Tactile masonry & timber thresholds
Deep brick reveals and custom white-oak pivot doors turn weather transitions into calm rooms.
Acoustic shelter on urban lots
Perimeter garden walls create quiet outdoor dining rooms even on compact city parcels.

props.text: New civic and studio life inside retained industrial shells.
Existing buildings hold irreplaceable embodied carbon, patina and spatial generosity. We audit structural capacity first and intervene with surgical restraint.
Embodied carbon preservation
Retaining foundation slabs, load-bearing masonry and heavy timber frames cuts project carbon by up to 65%.
Seismic & thermal upgrades
Concealed steel strongbacks and breathable wood-fiber insulation modernize envelopes without erasing character.
Daylight & acoustic calibration
Inserted roof monitors and timber slat baffles turn echoey warehouses into warm working halls.

props.text: Adaptive Reuse Dossier · Seattle Pioneer Square
Mercer Foundry Reading Room & Neighborhood Archive

Built in 1914 as a marine pattern shop, the Mercer building possessed 16-inch unreinforced brick walls and 48-foot old-growth Douglas fir king-post trusses. Rather than subdividing the volume, we inserted a free-standing white-oak mezzanine and opened the south masonry wall to a walled fern courtyard.
84% structural mass retained
Original brick perimeter, heavy-timber trusses and basalt foundation piers preserved in place.
Daylight factor 4.2% at reading tables
Continuous north skylight monitors provide glare-free illumination across 64 study carrels.
Seismic diaphragm & lime repointing
Concealed steel tie-rods and breathable hydraulic lime mortar extend building life by a century.
Discuss an existing building
Mass Timber Dossier · Oregon Coast Range
Nehalem Timber Pavilion & Rural Design Barn

Sited on an active regenerating forestry parcel above the Nehalem River, this two-volume workshop and residential studio pairs regionally harvested doweled Douglas fir frames with a thermal board-formed concrete base.
Deep 6-foot coastal roof overhangs
Protects untreated Western red cedar siding from winter driving rain while shading summer glass.
All-wood doweled portal frames
Prefabricated CNC timber bents erected in four days with zero structural steel weld plates.
Net-positive solar & rainwater harvest
14 kW standing-seam roof array and 18,000-gallon buried concrete cistern for year-round autonomy.

Monograph 014 · Residential Commission · Willamette Valley, OR
Alder Courtyard House: an open room at the center of the plan.

Designed for a multi-generational family on a wind-swept oak savanna ridge, this 2,850-square-foot residence gathers three single-story brick wings around a sheltered 32-by-38-foot gravel and Japanese maple courtyard.

props.alt: Pale-brick courtyard residence with oak-framed openings and planted gravel garden in morning light

props.text: Site & Orientation
Willamette Valley, OR · South-southeast ridge aspect
Gross Internal Area
2,850 sq ft conditioned · 1,216 sq ft sheltered court
Primary Envelope
Double-wythe Roman clay brick · Cavity wood-fiber insulation
Energy Performance
22 kBtu/sq ft/yr · Air-to-water heat pump & hydronic slab
Spatial thesis & daylight
Bringing the garden inward so every room touches the sky.

Conventional rural houses place a large footprint in the center of a clearing and look outward across exposed pastures. On this gusty ridge, we inverted the diagram: a continuous low Roman-brick wall deflects northwest winds while creating an intimate microclimate in the central court.

A glazed timber cloister walk connects the kitchen, library and bedroom wings. On mild mornings, 10-foot white-oak pivot doors swing open so the kitchen table and gravel court function as a single continuous room.
Borrowed light from two orientations
Balancing north courtyard glazing with deep-set south apertures eliminates daytime glare and electric lighting needs.
Acoustic separation for three generations
The guest and grandparent wing sits across the planted court from the main kitchen, linked by a covered brick loggia.
Honest lime-washed thermal mass
Interior brick wythes absorb low-angle winter sun and release radiant warmth through the evening.

props.text: The practice · Portland & Seattle
Attention to the ordinary rooms that hold a life.

Founded in 2016 by Julian Vance and Elena Rostova, Common Ground is a twelve-person architecture and adaptive reuse practice working from a converted 1922 brick seed warehouse in Portland’s Central Eastside.

We believe the most sustainable building is either one that already exists and is thoughtfully adapted, or a new building constructed with such material clarity and emotional resonance that future generations refuse to tear it down.
Explore our built works
How we structure commissions

props.text: Working principles
A practice built on observation, retention, and legible craft.
Before a drawing, there is a conversation at the site. Before a material specification, there is a physical sample tested in the light.
Listen to the existing place
We map microclimates, sun angles, mature trees and neighborhood cadence so new work feels anchored from its first season.
Retain useful fabric first
On every renovation or adaptive reuse site, we catalogue structural timbers, brickwork and stone that can carry forward into the new plan.
Shape rooms with natural light
We model daylight in physical 1:20 rooms so every primary space receives balanced illumination from at least two directions.
Detail for repair & longevity
Mechanical fasteners, lime mortars and solid timber joinery allow future stewards to maintain and adapt the building over decades.
Principals & project architects
Hands-on leadership from first site sketch to final punch list.
Every commission is co-led by a founding partner and a dedicated project architect who remain your direct points of contact throughout design and construction.

props.text: Architectural services & process
From an unhurried feasibility study to on-site craft supervision.
We structure our work in clear, sequential phases so you can test site constraints, spatial options and construction budgets before committing to full technical documentation.
Request a Phase I feasibility study
View built case studies
Five-phase architectural commission
A transparent sequence with clear deliverables at every milestone.
Clients may commission a standalone Phase I Feasibility Study before deciding how to proceed into full architectural design.
Phase I · Pre-Design & Existing Fabric Feasibility (4–6 Weeks)
We walk the site or laser-scan the existing building, audit zoning and environmental setbacks, evaluate structural retention potential, and establish a realistic project brief and target cost range.
Deliverables: Measured site/building survey, zoning & code dossier, two spatial massing options, and preliminary cost benchmark.
Phase II · Schematic Design & Physical Modeling (6–8 Weeks)
Working through hand drawings and a 1:20 basswood study model, we establish room relationships, courtyard orientation, structural grid and seasonal daylighting.
Deliverables: Schematic floor plans, site sections, 1:20 physical timber model, sun-path diagrams, and general contractor pricing check.
Phase III · Design Development & Material Mockups (8–10 Weeks)
We coordinate structural, mechanical and landscape engineers, refine custom cabinet and stair joinery, and review physical brick, mortar, stone and timber sample boards.
Deliverables: Coordinated architectural & engineering drawings, window/door schedule, outline specifications, and physical material sample box.
Phase IV · Permit & Technical Construction Documents (10–12 Weeks)
Comprehensive technical drawings and specifications for municipal permitting and binding builder bids, detailing every masonry flashing, thermal bridge and timber connection.
Deliverables: Stamped permit & construction drawing set, CSI specification manual, and contractor bid leveling.
Phase V · Construction Administration & Post-Occupancy

Weekly site walks alongside the builder to review shop drawings, approve on-site brick mortar panels and finish mockups, and verify system commissioning through move-in and a 12-month seasonal check-in.
Deliverables: Field observation reports, mockup approvals, punch-list verification, and owner maintenance dossier.

props.text: Preparing for our first meeting
Bring the place as it is today.
You do not need a finished floor plan or stylistic mood board to start. The most productive first conversations begin with four simple pieces of context:
Site address or parcel map
So we can review solar orientation, topography, tree canopy and municipal zoning overlays prior to our call.
Existing drawings or photographs
For renovations and adaptive reuse, even snapshots of exposed rafters, basement masonry or original blueprints are invaluable.
Daily routines & spatial priorities
Tell us how you cook, work, host guests or use outdoor space across wet winters and dry summers.
Target timeline & investment range
An honest early budget envelope lets us calibrate floor area and structural assembly from day one.
Commission FAQ
Common questions on fees, builders, and timelines.
Have a specific question about an unreinforced masonry building or rural land-use permit? Send us a note and a principal will reply within two business days.
Write to our principals

items.q: Can we hire Common Ground for a Phase I Feasibility Study before purchasing a property or warehouse?

items.a: We recommend selecting a craft-aligned general contractor on a negotiated pre-construction basis at the end of Schematic Design (Phase II). Early builder input on local masonry, timber sourcing and site logistics prevents budget surprises later.
items.q: When do you bring a general contractor into the process?

items.a: Yes. Built-in white-oak cabinetry, library shelving, lighting and courtyard threshold gardens are integral to our architectural scope, and we collaborate closely with regional landscape ecologists.
items.q: Do you coordinate interior architecture, custom millwork, and courtyard planting?

items.a: Our core practice area covers Oregon and Washington—from the Willamette Valley and Oregon Coast Range to Portland, Seattle and the Puget Sound islands.

First steps
What to expect after you reach out.
Whether you have a deeded site or are evaluating an existing building prior to purchase, our initial conversations are structured to give you clear, practical guidance.
Review our 5-phase service structure

items.a: Founding principals Julian Vance and Elena Rostova review your brief and site location within two business days, then schedule a complimentary 30-minute phone or studio consultation to discuss feasibility, zoning and project timeline.
items.q: What happens after I submit a project inquiry?

items.a: Yes. For sites within Portland, Seattle, the Willamette Valley or Puget Sound, we regularly conduct initial walks on site before preparing a fixed-fee Phase I Feasibility Study proposal.
items.q: Can we meet at our property or existing building for the initial consultation?

items.a: Frequently. Engaging an architect before closing on a rural parcel or historic masonry warehouse helps identify solar access, structural retention opportunities and permitting hurdles early.
items.q: Do you work with clients who are still comparing two or three parcels?
